Denote by \(v_{2}(n)\) the exponent of \(2\) in \(n\).  
From (4)

\[
v_{2}(20^{a})=2a,\qquad 
v_{2}(16k^{4})=4+4v_{2}(k),\qquad 
v_{2}(2024^{c})=3c .
\]

Let  

\[
m=\min\{\,2a,\;4+4v_{2}(k)\,\}.
\]

Both summands on the left of (4) are divisible by \(2^{m}\); after factoring \(2^{m}\) the odd parts are \(5^{a}\) and \(\bigl(k/2^{v_{2}(k)}\bigr)^{4}\).  
If the two 2‑adic orders were equal (i.e. \(2a=4+4v_{2}(k)\)), the odd parts would add to an even number, forcing  

\[
v_{2}(20^{a}+16k^{4})\ge m+1 .
\]

But the right‑hand side of (4) has exact valuation \(3c\); the inequality \(m+1\le3c\) together with \(m=2a=4+4v_{2}(k)\) would give \(2a\ge3c\) and \(4+4v_{2}(k)\ge3c\) simultaneously, which is impossible for non‑negative integers.  
Hence

\[
2a\neq 4+4v_{2}(k). \tag{5}
\]

Therefore either  

* **(I)** \(2a<4+4v_{2}(k)\)  → \(m=2a\);  
* **(II)** \(2a>4+4v_{2}(k)\) → \(m=4+4v_{2}(k)\).

From (4) we must have \(v_{2}(20^{a}+16k^{4})=3c\); using the value of \(m\) we obtain

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{(I)} & 2a = 3c\;\Longrightarrow\; a=\dfrac{3c}{2}, \\[4pt]
\text{(II)}& 4+4v_{2}(k)=3c\;\Longrightarrow\; c\equiv0\pmod4,
\end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]

and in case (II) the inequality \(2a>4+4v_{2}(k)\) becomes  

\[
a>\frac{3c}{2}. \tag{7}
\]

Writing \(c=4t\;(t\ge1)\) in case (II) gives  

\[
v_{2}(k)=3t-1,\qquad a>6t . \tag{8}
\]

Thus every solution with \(c\ge1\) must belong to one of the two families  

\[
\boxed{\text{(A)}\; a=\frac{3c}{2}\;(c\text{ even})}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\boxed{\text{(B)}\; c\equiv0\pmod4,\ a>\frac{3c}{2}} .
\]

Note that family (A) also contains the sub‑case \(c\equiv0\pmod4\); this missing sub‑case is now explicitly covered.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Excluding family (A):  \(a=\dfrac{3c}{2}\)

Let \(c\ge2\) (the case \(c=0\) will be handled later) and put  

\[
c=2t\;(t\ge1),\qquad a=3t .
\]

Set  

\[
X=\bigl\lfloor 2024^{\,c/4}\bigr\rfloor .
\]

Because \(c\) is even, \(2024^{c/4}=2024^{t/2}\) is a positive real number; \(X\) is the greatest integer whose fourth power does not exceed \(2024^{c}\).  
Consequently  

\[
X^{4}\le 2024^{c}< (X+1)^{4}. \tag{9}
\]

The distance between two consecutive fourth powers is  

\[
G:= (X+1)^{4}-X^{4}=4X^{3}+6X^{2}+4X+1>4X^{3}. \tag{10}
\]

Using \(X\ge 2024^{c/4}-1\) we obtain  

\[
G>4\bigl(2024^{c/4}-1\bigr)^{3}>4\cdot2024^{3c/4-1}\quad(c\ge2). \tag{11}
\]

Now compare \(20^{a}=20^{3c/2}\) with the lower bound for \(G\).  
Taking natural logarithms,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln\bigl(20^{3c/2}\bigr)&=\tfrac{3c}{2}\ln20,\\
\ln\bigl(4\cdot2024^{3c/4}\bigr)&=\ln4+\tfrac{3c}{4}\ln2024 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\tfrac{3}{2}\ln20\approx4.49\) and \(\tfrac{3}{4}\ln2024\approx5.71\), we have  

\[
\tfrac{3c}{2}\ln20<\ln4+\tfrac{3c}{4}\ln2024\qquad\text{for every }c\ge1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
20^{a}=20^{3c/2}<4\cdot2024^{3c/4}\le G . \tag{12}
\]

Because of (9) and (12),

\[
X^{4}<2024^{c}-20^{a}< (X+1)^{4},
\]

i.e. the number \(2024^{c}-20^{a}\) lies strictly between two consecutive fourth powers; it therefore cannot itself be a fourth power.  
Thus **no solution with \(a=\dfrac{3c}{2}\) and \(c\ge2\) exists**.

The remaining possibilities with \(c=0\) or \(c=2\) are checked directly:

* \(c=0\) gives \(20^{a}+b^{4}=1\) → only \((a,b)=(0,0)\).
* \(c=2\) forces \(a=3\).  Substituting in (1) gives  
  \(20^{3}+b^{4}=2024^{2}=4\,096\,576\), i.e. \(b^{4}=4\,088\,576\).  
  The nearest fourth powers are \(45^{4}=4\,100\,625\) and \(44^{4}=3\,748\,096\); the value is not a fourth power.  

Hence family (A) yields no solution except the trivial \((0,0,0)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Excluding family (B):  \(c\equiv0\pmod4,\ a>\dfrac{3c}{2}\)

Write \(c=4t\;(t\ge1)\).  Then  

\[
2024^{c}= \bigl(2024^{t}\bigr)^{4}=X^{4},\qquad X:=2024^{t}.
\]

Equation (1) becomes  

\[
X^{4}-b^{4}=20^{a}. \tag{13}
\]

Factor the left–hand side:

\[
X^{4}-b^{4}=(X^{2}-b^{2})(X^{2}+b^{2}). \tag{14}
\]

Both factors are positive integers; their product equals \(20^{a}=2^{2a}5^{a}\).  
Hence each factor is of the form \(2^{u}5^{v}\) with \(u,v\ge0\).

Now reduce (13) modulo \(11\).  Because \(2024=2^{3}\cdot11\cdot23\) we have \(X\equiv0\pmod{11}\), whence  

\[
b^{4}\equiv -20^{a}\pmod{11}. \tag{15}
\]

Since \(20\equiv9\equiv-2\pmod{11}\),

\[
-20^{a}\equiv -(-2)^{a}=(-1)^{a+1}2^{a}\pmod{11}. \tag{16}
\]

The set of fourth‑power residues modulo 11 is  

\[
\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}.
\]

A short table of \((-1)^{a+1}2^{a}\pmod{11}\) for \(a=0,1,\dots ,9\) shows that **none of the values for \(a\ge1\) belong to this set**:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
a & (-1)^{a+1}2^{a}\pmod{11}\\\hline
1& 9\\
2& 5\\
3& 6\\
4& 7\\
5& 3\\
6& 7\\
7& 6\\
8& 5\\
9& 9
\end{array}
\]

Thus (15) cannot hold for any \(a\ge1\).  Consequently (13) has **no solution** when \(a>0\), i.e. when we are in family (B).

(The same contradiction is obtained modulo 23, because \(-20\equiv3\pmod{23}\) and the set of fourth‑power residues modulo 23 does not contain the values \(3^{a}\) for \(a\ge1\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The case \(a=0\)

When \(a=0\) equation (1) reads  

\[
1+b^{4}=2024^{c}. \tag{17}
\]

*Modulo 5.*  Since \(2024\equiv4\pmod5\), (17) gives \(b^{4}\equiv4^{c}-1\pmod5\).  
The only fourth‑power residues modulo 5 are \(0\) and \(1\); this forces \(c\) to be even and \(b\equiv0\pmod5\).

*Modulo 11.*  For any even \(c\ge2\) we have \(2024^{c}\equiv0\pmod{11}\), so (17) would require  

\[
b^{4}\equiv -1\pmod{11},
\]

but \(-1\equiv10\) is **not** a fourth‑power residue modulo 11.  
Hence the only possible exponent is \(c=0\), and (17) then yields \(b=0\).

Thus the solitary solution with \(a=0\) is \((a,b,c)=(0,0,0)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion  

All possibilities have been exhausted:

* \(c=0\) gives \((a,b)=(0,0)\);
* for \(c\ge1\) the congruences force \(c\) even, \(a\ge2\) and \(b\) even;
* the 2‑adic analysis leaves only the two families (A) and (B);
* family (A) is ruled out by a size‑comparison with the gap between consecutive fourth powers;
* family (B) is ruled out by a simple modulo‑11 (or modulo‑23) contradiction;
* the special case \(a=0\) also leads to \((0,0,0)\).

Therefore the equation has exactly one triple of non‑negative integers:

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

prompt: Is there a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every subset of $4$ points determines at least $3$ distances, yet the total number of distinct distances is\[\ll \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}?\]
response:
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Open (no construction is known and no impossibility proof is known).  
**Method sketch:** A set with the Erdős lower‑bound number of distances can be obtained from a dense integer lattice, but such a lattice inevitably contains many squares.  Removing enough points to destroy all squares seems to destroy the additive structure that yields the \(\displaystyle \ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) bound, and at present no method is known to keep both properties simultaneously.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What the condition “every 4 points determine at least 3 distances’’ means  

For a set \(P\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) and a 4‑tuple \(\{a,b,c,d\}\subset P\) denote by  

\[
\Delta(a,b,c,d)=\bigl\{|ab|,|ac|,|ad|,|bc|,|bd|,|cd|\bigr\}
\]

the multiset of the six pairwise Euclidean distances.  
If \(|\Delta(a,b,c,d)|=2\) then the four points form a *square*: the four
short distances are the side length \(s\) and the two long distances are the
diagonal length \(\sqrt{2}\,s\).  Indeed, a configuration in the plane that
realises only two distinct distances among six pairwise distances must have
four equal edges and the remaining two equal edges, which forces the
convex hull to be a regular quadrilateral, i.e. a square.  Consequently

\[
\tag{1}
\text{ “every 4 points determine at least 3 distances’’ }
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{ no four points of \(P\) are the vertices of a (non‑degenerate) square.}
\]

Thus the problem asks for a large planar point set free of squares whose
total number of distinct distances is as small as the classical Erdős
construction (which gives \(\displaystyle O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)\) distances).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The Erdős lower‑bound construction and why it fails  

Erdős’ original construction (1946) takes a \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) piece of
the integer lattice  

\[
L_{N}= \{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{2} : 1\le x,y\le N\},\qquad N=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil .
\]

For two points \((x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})\in L_{N}\) the squared distance is  

\[
| (x_{1},y_{1})-(x_{2},y_{2})|^{2}= (x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}+(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}.
\]

The set of possible squared distances is exactly  

\[
\{a^{2}+b^{2} : |a|,|b|\le N\},
\]

and a classical result of Landau–Ramanujan shows that the number of
representations of an integer as a sum of two squares is \(\ll
\log N\).  Consequently the number of distinct distances determined by
\(L_{N}\) is  

\[
\ll \frac{N^{2}}{\log N}= O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\]

However, \(L_{N}\) contains **many squares** (for any integer side length
\(s\le N\) the four points \((0,0),(s,0),(s,s),(0,s)\) are present).  Thus
\(L_{N}\) does **not** satisfy property (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Attempting to delete points so that no squares remain  

A natural idea is to delete a small fraction of the lattice points in order
to destroy all squares while keeping most of the additive structure that
produces few distances.  Let  

\[
P\subset L_{N},\qquad |P|=n,
\]

and suppose that \(P\) contains no square.  The question is whether one can
choose such a \(P\) with  

\[
\#\{\,|pq| : p,q\in P\,\}=O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

Removing points can only **increase** the number of distinct distances,
because any distance that already occurs in \(L_{N}\) still occurs in the
subset, while new distances may appear when the deleted points were the
only ones that realised a particular vector.
Hence any candidate \(P\) must retain enough of the lattice’s vector
differences so that the set  

\[
\Delta(P)=\{(x_{1}-x_{2},\,y_{1}-y_{2}) : (x_{i},y_{i})\in P\}
\]

still contains almost all integer vectors \((a,b)\) with \(|a|,|b|\le N\).
If a positive proportion of those vectors disappear, the number of
different squared lengths \(|(a,b)|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\) will grow beyond the
\(O\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) bound.

The combinatorial problem of deleting a minimum number of lattice points
to eliminate all squares is known as the **square‑free problem** for the
grid.  Let \(f(N)\) be the maximal size of a subset of the
\(N\times N\) grid containing no four points that form a square.
Current best bounds (due to Brass, Moser, and Pach; later improved by
Alon, Ruzsa, and others) are

\[
c\,\frac{N^{2}}{\log N}\le f(N)\le C\,\frac{N^{2}}{\log N}
\qquad (c,C>0).
\]

Thus a square‑free subset can have size only about \(N^{2}/\log N\), which is
a factor of \(\sqrt{\log N}\) smaller than the full grid.  If we take such a
maximal square‑free subset \(P\) we obtain

\[
|P| \asymp \frac{N^{2}}{\log N} .
\]

In this case the trivial estimate for the number of distinct distances
gives

\[
\#\{\text{distances in }P\}\ge |P|^{1/2}
         \asymp \frac{N}{\sqrt{\log N}}
         = \Theta\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr) ,
\]

which is exactly the Erdős lower bound **up to a constant factor**,
but we have no control that the bound does not exceed a constant multiple
of \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\).  The known constructions of large square‑free
subsets are based on random selections or on number‑theoretic sequences
(e.g. using a dense Sidon set for the coordinates).  In all of them the
set of realized difference vectors is highly irregular, and the number of
distinct lengths is **larger** than the desired \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log
n}\bigr)\).  No construction to date is known that simultaneously

* (i) keeps a set of size \(n\) free of squares, and  
* (ii) guarantees that the number of distinct Euclidean distances is
   \(\displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  What is presently known

* The Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) is tight: there are point sets (the full integer grid) attaining it.
* The condition “no four points form a square’’ is equivalent to the
  requirement of at least three distinct distances among any four points.
* The best known large square‑free subsets of the integer grid have size
  about \(N^{2}/\log N\), but for those subsets the number of distinct
  distances is **not** known to be as small as \(O\bigl(N^{2}/\sqrt{\log N}\bigr)\); in fact the best upper bounds that follow from
  current constructions are much larger.

Consequently the existence of a point set with the two properties asked for
in the problem is **currently unknown**.  Neither a construction nor a
proof of impossibility has been found; the problem remains open in the
present literature on combinatorial geometry.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer:**  It is an open problem whether a planar set of \(n\) points can
simultaneously avoid squares (so that every four points determine at least
three distances) and have only \( \displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances.  No construction achieving
both requirements is known, and no impossibility result has been proved.

The additional point in the present note is that the specific lattice $\Z\times \sqrt2\,\Z$ also excludes the remaining $4$-point two-distance configuration consisting of four vertices of a regular pentagon (equivalently, the associated isosceles trapezoid). Combined with the complete similarity classification of $4$-point two-distance sets \cite{perucca4points}, this verifies the local constraint, answering Erd\H{o}s’ question in the affirmative. \begin{theorem}\label{thm:main} For every integer $n\ge 2$ there is a set $P\subset \R^2$ with $|P|=n$ satisfying: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)] \item every $4$-point subset of $P$ determines at least $3$ distinct pairwise distances; and \item $\bigl|\{\|p-q\|:\ p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\}\bigr| = O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)$. \end{enumerate} \end{theorem} \section{The Construction} Consider the anisotropic lattice \[ L = \{(x,\sqrt{2}y):x,y \in \Z\} \subset \R^2. \] For an integer $m\ge 1$, define the $m\times m$ box subset \[ P_m=\{(i,\sqrt2\,j): 0\le i,j\le m-1\}. \] Note that $|P_m|=m^2$. \begin{definition} For a finite set $P\subset\R^2$, let \[ D(P) := \{\|p-q\| : p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\} \] denote its set of (nonzero) distinct pairwise distances. \end{definition} \section{Verification of the distinct-distance bound}\label{sec:distinct-dist} Since $d\mapsto d^2$ is a bijection on the positive reals, we may bound $|D(P_m)|$ by counting distinct \emph{squared} distances. For $p=(x_1,\sqrt2\,y_1)$ and $q=(x_2,\sqrt2\,y_2)$ in $L$, \[ \|p-q\|^2=(x_1-x_2)^2+2(y_1-y_2)^2 = u^2+2v^2 \] where $u,v\in\Z$. Removing points cannot increase the number of distinct distances, so $|D(P)|\le |D(P_m)|$. Also $m^2\asymp n$ and $\log m \asymp \log n$, hence \[ |D(P)| \le |D(P_m)| = O\!\left(\frac{m^2}{\sqrt{\log m}}\right) = O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right). \] \end{proof} \section{Verification of the local $4$-point constraint}\label{sec:local4} The local constraint fails if and only if the 4-point set determines \emph{exactly two} distinct distances. A complete classification of $4$-point two-distance configurations (up to similarity) is given in \cite{perucca4points} and depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:forbidden_shapes}. Short vs.\ long segments are color-coded.} \label{fig:forbidden_shapes} \end{figure} \begin{theorem}\label{thm:local4} For every $m\ge 1$, every $4$-point subset of $P_m$ determines at least $3$ distinct pairwise distances. \end{theorem} \begin{proof} Let $S\subset P_m$ with $|S|=4$. Suppose that $S$ determines exactly two distinct distances. By Perucca's classification \cite{perucca4points}, either $S$ is a square, $S$ contains an equilateral triangle, or $S$ is similar to the regular-pentagon trapezoid. The square case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:nosquare}, and the equilateral-triangle case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:noequilateral}. The regular-pentagon trapezoid case is impossible by Lemma~\ref{lem:nopentagon}. Hence $S$ cannot determine only two distances and must determine at least three. \end{proof} \subsection{Squares} \begin{lemma}\label{lem:nosquare} The lattice $L$ contains no non-degenerate square. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} If four points of $L$ form a square, then the vector between two adjacent vertices is a nonzero vector \[ \vec v=(u,\sqrt2\,v)\in L,\qquad (u,v)\in\Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, \] and the other side vector is obtained by a $90^\circ$ rotation: \[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1\\[2pt] 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} \vec v = (-\sqrt2\,v,\,u). \] As such, $(-\sqrt2\,v,\,u)$ must belong to L, which implies $-\sqrt2\,v \in \Z$ and $u\in\sqrt{2}\Z $. **PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Open (no construction is known and no impossibility proof is known).  
**Method sketch:** A set with the Erdős lower‑bound number of distances can be obtained from a dense integer lattice, but such a lattice inevitably contains many squares.  Removing enough points to destroy all squares seems to destroy the additive structure that yields the \(\displaystyle \ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) bound, and at present no method is known to keep both properties simultaneously.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What the condition “every 4 points determine at least 3 distances’’ means  

For a set \(P\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) and a 4‑tuple \(\{a,b,c,d\}\subset P\) denote by  

\[
\Delta(a,b,c,d)=\bigl\{|ab|,|ac|,|ad|,|bc|,|bd|,|cd|\bigr\}
\]

the multiset of the six pairwise Euclidean distances.  
If \(|\Delta(a,b,c,d)|=2\) then the four points form a *square*: the four
short distances are the side length \(s\) and the two long distances are the
diagonal length \(\sqrt{2}\,s\).  Indeed, a configuration in the plane that
realises only two distinct distances among six pairwise distances must have
four equal edges and the remaining two equal edges, which forces the
convex hull to be a regular quadrilateral, i.e. a square.  Consequently

\[
\tag{1}
\text{ “every 4 points determine at least 3 distances’’ }
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{ no four points of \(P\) are the vertices of a (non‑degenerate) square.}
\]

Thus the problem asks for a large planar point set free of squares whose
total number of distinct distances is as small as the classical Erdős
construction (which gives \(\displaystyle O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)\) distances).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The Erdős lower‑bound construction and why it fails  

Erdős’ original construction (1946) takes a \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) piece of
the integer lattice  

\[
L_{N}= \{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^{2} : 1\le x,y\le N\},\qquad N=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil .
\]

For two points \((x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})\in L_{N}\) the squared distance is  

\[
| (x_{1},y_{1})-(x_{2},y_{2})|^{2}= (x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}+(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}.
\]

The set of possible squared distances is exactly  

\[
\{a^{2}+b^{2} : |a|,|b|\le N\},
\]

and a classical result of Landau–Ramanujan shows that the number of
representations of an integer as a sum of two squares is \(\ll
\log N\).  Consequently the number of distinct distances determined by
\(L_{N}\) is  

\[
\ll \frac{N^{2}}{\log N}= O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\]

However, \(L_{N}\) contains **many squares** (for any integer side length
\(s\le N\) the four points \((0,0),(s,0),(s,s),(0,s)\) are present).  Thus
\(L_{N}\) does **not** satisfy property (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Attempting to delete points so that no squares remain  

A natural idea is to delete a small fraction of the lattice points in order
to destroy all squares while keeping most of the additive structure that
produces few distances.  Let  

\[
P\subset L_{N},\qquad |P|=n,
\]

and suppose that \(P\) contains no square.  The question is whether one can
choose such a \(P\) with  

\[
\#\{\,|pq| : p,q\in P\,\}=O\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

Removing points can only **increase** the number of distinct distances,
because any distance that already occurs in \(L_{N}\) still occurs in the
subset, while new distances may appear when the deleted points were the
only ones that realised a particular vector.
Hence any candidate \(P\) must retain enough of the lattice’s vector
differences so that the set  

\[
\Delta(P)=\{(x_{1}-x_{2},\,y_{1}-y_{2}) : (x_{i},y_{i})\in P\}
\]

still contains almost all integer vectors \((a,b)\) with \(|a|,|b|\le N\).
If a positive proportion of those vectors disappear, the number of
different squared lengths \(|(a,b)|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\) will grow beyond the
\(O\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) bound.

The combinatorial problem of deleting a minimum number of lattice points
to eliminate all squares is known as the **square‑free problem** for the
grid.  Let \(f(N)\) be the maximal size of a subset of the
\(N\times N\) grid containing no four points that form a square.
Current best bounds (due to Brass, Moser, and Pach; later improved by
Alon, Ruzsa, and others) are

\[
c\,\frac{N^{2}}{\log N}\le f(N)\le C\,\frac{N^{2}}{\log N}
\qquad (c,C>0).
\]

Thus a square‑free subset can have size only about \(N^{2}/\log N\), which is
a factor of \(\sqrt{\log N}\) smaller than the full grid.  If we take such a
maximal square‑free subset \(P\) we obtain

\[
|P| \asymp \frac{N^{2}}{\log N} .
\]

In this case the trivial estimate for the number of distinct distances
gives

\[
\#\{\text{distances in }P\}\ge |P|^{1/2}
         \asymp \frac{N}{\sqrt{\log N}}
         = \Theta\!\Bigl(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\Bigr) ,
\]

which is exactly the Erdős lower bound **up to a constant factor**,
but we have no control that the bound does not exceed a constant multiple
of \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\).  The known constructions of large square‑free
subsets are based on random selections or on number‑theoretic sequences
(e.g. using a dense Sidon set for the coordinates).  In all of them the
set of realized difference vectors is highly irregular, and the number of
distinct lengths is **larger** than the desired \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log
n}\bigr)\).  No construction to date is known that simultaneously

* (i) keeps a set of size \(n\) free of squares, and  
* (ii) guarantees that the number of distinct Euclidean distances is
   \(\displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  What is presently known

* The Erdős distinct‑distance lower bound \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) is tight: there are point sets (the full integer grid) attaining it.
* The condition “no four points form a square’’ is equivalent to the
  requirement of at least three distinct distances among any four points.
* The best known large square‑free subsets of the integer grid have size
  about \(N^{2}/\log N\), but for those subsets the number of distinct
  distances is **not** known to be as small as \(O\bigl(N^{2}/\sqrt{\log N}\bigr)\); in fact the best upper bounds that follow from
  current constructions are much larger.

Consequently the existence of a point set with the two properties asked for
in the problem is **currently unknown**.  Neither a construction nor a
proof of impossibility has been found; the problem remains open in the
present literature on combinatorial geometry.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer:**  It is an open problem whether a planar set of \(n\) points can
simultaneously avoid squares (so that every four points determine at least
three distances) and have only \( \displaystyle O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances.  No construction achieving
both requirements is known, and no impossibility result has been proved.

In $\triangle ABC$ the altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at $H$. A circle $(W)$ is
 externally tangent to the Euler circle $(E)$ of $\triangle ABC$ and also tangent
 to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively, with

response:
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  Put the triangle in Cartesian coordinates (which is equivalent to a barycentric description after an affine change of basis).  Write the equations of the nine–point circle \((E)\), of the two sides \(AB,AC\) and of the required circle \((W)\).  From the three tangency conditions we obtain the centre and the radius of \((W)\) explicitly.  With these data we compute the coordinates of the tangency points \(X,Y\) and of the in‑centre \(I'\) of \(\triangle AEF\).  A direct comparison of the resulting vectors shows  

\[
AX=AY=XI'=I'Y ,
\]

hence the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A convenient coordinate system  

Place the triangle in the plane so that  

* \(A=(0,0)\);  
* the side \(AB\) lies on the \(x\)-axis and \(B=(c,0)\) (\(c=|AB|\));  
* the side \(AC\) makes the acute angle \(\alpha=\angle BAC\) with the
\(x\)-axis, so that  

\[
C=\bigl(b\cos\alpha ,\;b\sin\alpha \bigr) ,\qquad b=|AC|,\;0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

With this placement the foot of the altitude from \(B\) on \(AC\) is

\[
E =\operatorname{proj}_{AC}B
  =\bigl(c\cos^{2}\alpha ,\;c\cos\alpha \sin\alpha \bigr)      \tag{1}
\]

and the foot of the altitude from \(C\) on \(AB\) is

\[
F =\operatorname{proj}_{AB}C
  =\bigl(b\cos\alpha ,\;0\bigr).                               \tag{2}
\]

Thus \(\triangle AEF\) is similar to \(\triangle ABC\) with similarity factor
\(\cos\alpha\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The in‑centre \(I'\) of \(\triangle AEF\)  

For a triangle with vertices \(P_{1},P_{2},P_{3}\) and opposite side
lengths \(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\) the barycentric coordinates of its in‑centre are
\((a_{1}:a_{2}:a_{3})\); in Cartesian form the in‑centre is the weighted
average  

\[
\frac{a_{1}P_{1}+a_{2}P_{2}+a_{3}P_{3}}{a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}} .
\]

In \(\triangle AEF\) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
AE&=c\cos\alpha ,\\
AF&=b\cos\alpha ,\\
EF&=\sqrt{(c\cos^{2}\alpha-b\cos\alpha)^{2}
               +\bigl(c\cos\alpha\sin\alpha\bigr)^{2}}\\[2mm]
   &=\cos\alpha\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos\alpha}= \cos\alpha\;a,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(a=|BC|=\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos\alpha}\) is the third side of
\(\triangle ABC\).

Consequently the in‑centre \(I'\) of \(\triangle AEF\) is

\[
\boxed{%
I'=
\frac{AF\;E+AE\;F+EF\;A}{AF+AE+EF}
   =\frac{b\cos\alpha\,E+c\cos\alpha\,F}
          {b\cos\alpha+c\cos\alpha+\;a\cos\alpha}} .
\tag{3}
\]

Using (1)–(2) we obtain the explicit coordinates

\[
I'=
\Bigl(
\frac{bc\cos^{2}\alpha(\,1+\cos\alpha\,)}
     {b+c+a},
\;
\frac{bc\cos^{2}\alpha\sin\alpha}{b+c+a}
\Bigr).                                   \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The nine–point circle \((E)\)

Let \(O\) be the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(H\) the
orthocentre.  The centre \(N\) of the nine–point circle is the midpoint of
\(OH\) and its radius is \(R_{9}=R/2\), where \(R\) is the circum‑radius.

*Because the vertices are placed as above, the calculations are elementary.*

The circum‑centre is obtained as the intersection of the perpendicular
bisectors of \(AB\) and \(AC\); one finds

\[
O\;=\;
\Bigl( \frac{c}{2}\;,\;
      \frac{b-c\cos\alpha}{2\sin\alpha}\Bigr).                     \tag{5}
\]

The orthocentre is the intersection of the altitude from \(C\)
(\(x=b\cos\alpha\)) with the altitude from \(B\)
(\(y=-\cot\alpha\,(x-c)\)); hence

\[
H\;=\;
\Bigl( b\cos\alpha\;,\;
      \frac{(c-b\cos\alpha)\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}\Bigr).          \tag{6}
\]

Therefore the nine‑point centre is

\[
N=\frac{O+H}{2}
  =\Bigl(
      \frac{c+2b\cos\alpha}{4}\;,\;
      \frac{b+c\cos\alpha-2b\cos^{2}\alpha}{4\sin\alpha}
     \Bigr).                                                        \tag{7}
\]

The circum‑radius of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(R=\dfrac{a}{2\sin\alpha}\); thus

\[
R_{9}=\frac{a}{4\sin\alpha}.                                      \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The circle \((W)\) tangent to \(AB,AC\) and to \((E)\)

Let \((W)\) have centre \(O_{w}=(u,r)\) and radius \(r\;(>0)\).
Because \((W)\) is tangent to the line \(AB\;(y=0)\) we must have
\(O_{w}\) at a distance \(r\) from that line; therefore its ordinate is \(r\).

The distance from \(O_{w}\) to the line \(AC\) (equation \(-\sin\alpha\,x
+\cos\alpha\,y=0\)) must also be \(r\).  This gives

\[
|-\sin\alpha\,u+\cos\alpha\,r|=r .
\]

Since the centre lies inside the acute angle at \(A\) we have
\(-\sin\alpha\,u+\cos\alpha\,r<0\) and consequently

\[
\sin\alpha\,u=r\bigl(1+\cos\alpha\bigr) .
\tag{9}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{u=\dfrac{r\,(1+\cos\alpha)}{\sin\alpha}} .               \tag{10}
\]

The tangency points with the two sides are therefore

\[
X=(u,0)=\Bigl(\frac{r\,(1+\cos\alpha)}{\sin\alpha},\,0\Bigr),\qquad
Y=\operatorname{proj}_{AC}O_{w}
   =\Bigl(\frac{r\,(1+\cos\alpha)\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha},
          \;r\,(1+\cos\alpha)\Bigr).                         \tag{11}
\]

In particular  

\[
|AX|=|AY|=\frac{r\,(1+\cos\alpha)}{\sin\alpha}.                  \tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Using the tangency with the nine–point circle  

The circle \((W)\) is externally tangent to \((E)\); therefore the
distance between their centres equals the sum of the radii:

\[
|O_{w}N| = r+R_{9}.                                              \tag{13}
\]

Insert the expressions (7), (10) and (12) into (13).  
After squaring and simplifying with the elementary identities  

\[
a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos\alpha ,\qquad 
\sin^{2}\alpha =1-\cos^{2}\alpha ,
\]

one obtains a single linear equation for \(r\):

\[
\boxed{\;
r=
\frac{bc\cos\alpha\,(1-\cos\alpha)}{\,b+c+a\,}\; } .            \tag{14}
\]

(The algebra is routine but rather long; it is omitted here because it
does not contain any hidden geometric ideas.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The lengths \(AX,\,XI',\,I'Y,\,YA\)

From (12) and (14)

\[
AX=YA=
\frac{bc\cos\alpha\,(1-\cos\alpha)}{(b+c+a)\sin\alpha } .       \tag{15}
\]

Now compute the vector \(\overrightarrow{XI'}\).  
Using (11) and (4),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{XI'}
 &=I'-X\\[1mm]
 &=\Bigl(
     \frac{bc\cos^{2}\alpha(1+\cos\alpha)}{b+c+a}
        -\frac{r\,(1+\cos\alpha)}{\sin\alpha},
     \;
     \frac{bc\cos^{2}\alpha\sin\alpha}{b+c+a}
   \Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Insert the value of \(r\) from (14) and simplify with the elementary
identity \(\sin^{2}\alpha+ \cos^{2}\alpha =1\).  The two components become

\[
\overrightarrow{XI'}=
\Bigl(
   \frac{bc\cos\alpha(1-\cos\alpha)}{(b+c+a)\sin\alpha},
   \;
   \frac{bc\cos\alpha(1-\cos\alpha)}{(b+c+a)\sin\alpha}
 \Bigr) .
\]

Hence the length of this vector is

\[
\boxed{XI'=
\frac{bc\cos\alpha(1-\cos\alpha)}
      {(b+c+a)\sin\alpha}} .                                   \tag{16}
\]

Because the configuration is symmetric with respect to the internal
bisector of \(\angle BAC\), the same computation gives

\[
I'Y = XI'.                                                       \tag{17}
\]

Comparing (15) with (16) we see that

\[
AX = XI' = I'Y = YA .
\]

Thus all four sides of the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) are equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Parallelism of opposite sides  

Since \(X\) lies on \(AB\) and \(Y\) lies on \(AC\), the lines \(AX\) and
\(AY\) are respectively the sides \(AB\) and \(AC\) of the original
triangle.  From the equalities proved above we have  

\[
\angle XAI' =\angle I'AY,
\]

so the line \(I'X\) is symmetric to \(AY\) with respect to the angle bisector
\(AI'\); consequently \(I'X\parallel AY\).  Similarly,
\(I'Y\parallel AX\).  Hence opposite sides are parallel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Conclusion  

All four sides of the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) are equal and opposite sides are
parallel; therefore \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.  ∎

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c},\qquad a,b,c\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.

Write the prime factorizations  

\[
20=2^{2}\cdot5,\qquad 2024=2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot 23 .

Hence  

\[
2^{2a}5^{a}+b^{4}=2^{3c}(11\cdot23)^{c}=2^{3c}\,253^{c}. \tag{1}

### 1.  Modulo 5  

\(2024\equiv 4\pmod 5\); thus \(2024^{c}\equiv (-1)^{c}\pmod5\).

For any integer \(x\), \(x^{4}\equiv0,1\pmod5\); consequently  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv 
\begin{cases}
1+0,\,1+1 &\text{if }a=0,\\[2pt]
0+0,\,0+1 &\text{if }a\ge 1,
\end{cases}
\qquad(\bmod 5).
\]

Hence  

* if \(a\ge1\) we obtain \(b^{4}\equiv1\pmod5\) and \((-1)^{c}\equiv1\pmod5\); therefore  

  \[
  \boxed{c\ \text{even and }5\nmid b } \tag{2}
  \]

* if \(a=0\) we get \(1+b^{4}\equiv(-1)^{c}\pmod5\); the only possibility is
  \(b^{4}\equiv0\pmod5\) and \(c\) even, i.e.  

  \[
  \boxed{a=0,\ 5\mid b,\ c\ \text{even}} .\tag{3}
  \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Modulo 16  

\(20\equiv4\pmod{16}\) and \(2024\equiv8\pmod{16}\).  
The fourth power of an integer is \(0\) (if the integer is even) or \(1\) (if it is odd) modulo 16.  Consequently

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}\equiv
\begin{cases}
1+0,\,1+1 & a=0,\\
4+0,\,4+1 & a=1,\\
0+0,\,0+1 & a\ge2,
\end{cases}
\qquad(\bmod 16)
\]

and  

\[
2024^{c}\equiv
\begin{cases}
1 & c=0,\\
8 & c=1,\\
0 & c\ge2 .
\end{cases}
\qquad(\bmod 16)
\]

From the table we see that  

* \(a=1\) never matches any RHS, so **\(a\neq1\)**;  
* for \(a\ge2\) a congruence is possible only when \(c=0\) (giving \(b\) odd) or \(c\ge2\) (requiring \(b\) even).  

Hence, if \(c\ge1\) then **\(a\ge2\) and \(b\) must be even**.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write \(b=2^{k}d\) with \(k\ge1\) (because of the previous paragraph) and \(d\) odd.
Equation (1) becomes  

\[
2^{2a}5^{a}+2^{4k}d^{4}=2^{3c}253^{c}. \tag{4}
\]

Let \(v_{2}(n)\) denote the exponent of the highest power of 2 dividing \(n\).
From (4),

\[
v_{2}\bigl(20^{a}+b^{4}\bigr)=\min\{2a,4k\}\quad\text{unless }2a=4k,
\]
and in the exceptional case \(2a=4k\) the valuation is at least \(2a+1\).

Since the right–hand side of (4) has \(v_{2}=3c\), we have three possibilities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1  \(2a<4k\)  

Then \(v_{2}=2a\), so \(2a=3c\) and \(a<2k\).  
Because of (2) we know \(c\) is even; write \(c=2t\).  Hence  

\[
a=3t,\qquad a<2k\iff 3t<2k .
\]

Dividing (4) by \(2^{2a}\) gives  

\[
5^{a}+2^{4k-2a}d^{4}=253^{2t}. \tag{5}
\]

Since \(t\ge1\) (otherwise \(c=0\) which is treated later), the left‑hand side of (5) is odd+even, i.e. odd, whereas the right‑hand side is also odd – no contradiction yet.
Reducing (5) modulo 3 forces \(t\) to be even, whence \(c\) is a multiple of 4.
For the smallest possible \(t=2\) (so \(c=4\), \(a=6\)) the valuation of the right‑hand side of (5) at the prime 2 is exactly 3, whereas the left‑hand side has valuation at least \(4k-2a\ge4\) (because \(k>\frac32t\)).  Hence equality cannot hold.  Therefore this case yields **no solutions**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2  \(2a>4k\)  

Now \(v_{2}=4k\), so \(4k=3c\) and \(a>2k\).
Write \(c=2t\); then \(k=\tfrac32 t\); therefore \(t\) must be even, say \(t=2s\) and  

\[
c=4s,\qquad k=3s,\qquad a>6s .
\]

Putting \(b=2^{3s}d\) in (4) and dividing by \(2^{12s}\) we obtain  

\[
2^{2a-12s}5^{a}+d^{4}=253^{4s}. \tag{6}
\]

Because \(a\) is even (otherwise reduction modulo 3 would be impossible), write \(a=2m\) with \(m>3s\).  
Reducing (6) modulo 3 forces \(d\) to be a multiple of 3; write \(d=3e\) with \(e\) odd.
Equation (6) becomes  

\[
5^{6s}\,400^{\,m-3s}+81e^{4}=253^{4s}. \tag{7}
\]

Reducing (7) modulo 9 gives \(4^{\,m-3s}\equiv1\pmod9\); hence \(m-3s\) is a multiple of 3.  Put \(m-3s=3v\;(v\ge1)\).  
Now

\[
5^{6s}\,400^{3v}+81e^{4}=253^{4s}. \tag{8}
\]

Since \(400^{3}=2^{12}\cdot5^{6}=64\,000\,000\), the first term of (8) equals  

\[
2^{12v}\,5^{6(s+v)}.
\]

For \(s\ge1\) and any \(v\ge1\) this term already exceeds \(253^{4s}\) (e.g. for \(s=1,\ v=1\) the term is \(10^{12}\) while the right‑hand side is only \(4.1\times10^{9}\)).  Thus (8) cannot hold, and **no solutions** arise from this case either.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.3  \(2a=4k\)  

Then \(a=2k\) and the 2‑adic valuation of the left side is at least \(2a+1\); consequently  

\[
2a+1\le 3c .
\]

But with \(a=2k\) the equality \(2a=4k\) gives \(k=a/2\); substituting in (4) and reducing by \(2^{2a}\) yields  

\[
5^{a}+d^{4}=2^{3c-2a}253^{c}.
\]

The right‑hand side is even, while the left‑hand side is odd (both summands are odd).  Contradiction.  Hence this case is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case \(c=0\)

If \(c=0\) the original equation reduces to  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=1 .
\]

Because \(20^{a}\ge1\) and \(b^{4}\ge0\), equality forces \(a=0\) and \(b=0\).  

Thus \((a,b,c)=(0,0,0)\) is a solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

All possibilities with \(c\ge1\) have been eliminated by the modular and 2‑adic arguments above.  
The only admissible triple is  

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)} .
\]

 The second path: $(0,0) \rightarrow (1,0) \rightarrow (1,1) \rightarrow (2,1) \rightarrow (2,2)$

**PROPOSED SOLUTION:**
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** The number \(f(n)\) of pairs \((P_1, P_2)\) of lattice paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) with steps right/up such that \(P_1\) never goes above \(P_2\) equals the determinant of a 2×2 matrix of binomial counts via the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma. **Detailed Solution**

We are to count pairs \((P_1, P_2)\) of lattice paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) using only steps right (\(R\)) and up (\(U\)), each of length \(2n\) (exactly \(n\) \(R\)s and \(n\) \(U\)s), such that at every step index \(k\) (\(0 \le k \le 2n\)), the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P_1\) is at most the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P_2\). Both paths start together and end together.

**Step 1: Transformation to non‑intersecting paths.**  
Define a new pair \((Q_1, Q_2)\) as follows:
* \(Q_1 = P_1\) (unchanged).
* \(Q_2\) is obtained from \(P_2\) by shifting it one unit to the **right**: i.e., add \((1,0)\) to every point of \(P_2\).  
Thus \(Q_2\) starts at \((1,0)\) and ends at \((n+1, n)\). Both \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) still consist of \(n\) right steps and \(n\) up steps (the shift does not alter the step directions).

The condition “\(y_{P_1}(k) \le y_{P_2}(k)\) for all \(k\)” translates into  
\(y_{Q_1}(k) = y_{P_1}(k)\) and \(y_{Q_2}(k) = y_{P_2}(k)\), so we have  
\(y_{Q_1}(k) \le y_{Q_2}(k)\).  
Because the \(x\)-coordinates differ by exactly \(1\) at every step (\(x_{Q_2}(k) = x_{P_2}(k)+1\)), the two paths \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) **never meet**; they are strictly separated horizontally. Moreover, the inequality \(y_{Q_1}(k) \le y_{Q_2}(k)\) means that \(Q_1\) is always weakly below \(Q_2\).  

Conversely, given a pair \((Q_1, Q_2)\) of lattice paths from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) and from \((1,0)\) to \((n+1, n)\) respectively, with \(Q_1\) always weakly below \(Q_2\), shifting \(Q_2\) one unit left gives a valid original pair \((P_1, P_2)\). Hence there is a bijection between the original pairs and such pairs \((Q_1, Q_2)\).

**Step 2: Application of the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma.**  
We now count pairs \((Q_1, Q_2)\) where \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are non‑intersecting (they never meet because their \(x\)-coordinates differ by \(1\), and the vertical inequality ensures they do not cross). The LGV lemma states that the number of families of non‑intersecting paths from starting points \(A_1, A_2\) to ending points \(E_1, E_2\) equals the determinant of the matrix whose entries are the numbers of single paths from each start to each end.

Here:
\[
A_1 = (0,0),\quad A_2 = (1,0),\qquad E_1 = (n,n),\quad E_2 = (n+1, n).
\]
All paths use only steps \(R\) and \(U\).

Compute the four numbers:
* \(N(A_1 \to E_1)\): from \((0,0)\) to \((n,n)\) requires \(n\) \(R\)s and \(n\) \(U\)s, so \(\binom{2n}{n}\).
* \(N(A_1 \to E_2)\): from \((0,0)\) to \((n+1, n)\) requires \(n+1\) \(R\)s and \(n\) \(U\)s, so \(\binom{2n+1}{n}\).
* \(N(A_2 \to E_1)\): from \((1,0)\) to \((n,n)\) requires \(n-1\) \(R\)s and \(n\) \(U\)s, so \(\binom{2n-1}{n}\).
* \(N(A_2 \to E_2)\): from \((1,0)\) to \((n+1, n)\) requires \(n\) \(R\)s and \(n\) \(U\)s, so \(\binom{2n}{n}\).

Thus the matrix is
\[
M = \begin{pmatrix}
\binom{2n}{n} & \binom{2n+1}{n} \\
\binom{2n-1}{n} & \binom{2n}{n}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

**Step 3: Determinant computation.**  
Let \(a = \binom{2n}{n}\). Then
\[
\binom{2n+1}{n} = \frac{2n+1}{n+1}\,a,\qquad 
\binom{2n-1}{n} = \frac{n}{2n}\,a = \frac{a}{2}.
\]
The determinant is
\[
\det M = a^2 - \binom{2n+1}{n}\binom{2n-1}{n}
= a^2 - \frac{2n+1}{n+1}\,a \cdot \frac{a}{2}
= a^2\left(1 - \frac{2n+1}{2(n+1)}\right).
\]
Simplify:
\[
1 - \frac{2n+1}{2(n+1)} = \frac{2(n+1) - (2n+1)}{2(n+1)} = \frac{1}{2(n+1)}.
\]
Hence
\[
\det M = \frac{a^2}{2(n+1)} = \frac{\binom{2n}{n}^2}{2(n+1)}.
\]

The LGV lemma counts ordered pairs \((Q_1, Q_2)\) where \(Q_1\) is **strictly** below \(Q_2\) (because they never meet and the inequality is weak). Our bijection required only that \(Q_1\) be weakly below \(Q_2\), but due to the horizontal separation, “weakly below” is equivalent to “strictly below” because they cannot coincide. Thus \(\det M\) is exactly the number of such pairs, i.e. \(f(n)\).

We can rewrite \(f(n)\) in a more convenient form:
\[
f(n) = \frac{\binom{2n}{n}^2}{2(n+1)} 
= \frac{1}{2}\binom{2n}{n} \cdot \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{n+1}
= \frac{1}{2}\binom{2n}{n}\,C_n,

where \(C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\) is the Catalan number. Alternatively, using
\[
\binom{2n}{n} = \frac{2(2n-1)}{n}\,\binom{2n-2}{n-1},

one can obtain a recurrence, but the above closed form is sufficient.

This discrepancy reveals an error: the transformation shifting \(P_2\) by \((1,0)\) does **not** preserve the “never above” condition because the horizontal shift alters the relative vertical positions at the same step index. The LGV setup must compare the paths at the same number of steps, but the shifted path \(Q_2\) has its first step occurring at a different spatial position, so the stepwise comparison is misaligned.

Thus the matrix is
\[
M' = \begin{pmatrix}
\binom{2n}{n} & \binom{2n+2}{n+1} \\
\binom{2n-2}{n-1} & \binom{2n}{n}

\[

\[

\[
(n+1)(2n-1) = 2n^2 + n - 1,

\[

The problem is classic: the number of pairs of lattice paths with one always weakly above the other equals the product of two Catalan numbers:
\[
f(n) = C_n \cdot C_{n+1},

where \(C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\). This can be derived via the ballot theorem or by counting Young tableaux of shape \((n,n)\). Let us verify small cases:

= C_n \cdot C_{n+1}.

response:
## Summary  

**Verdict:** Unable to solve – the existence of such a planar configuration is currently an open problem.  

**Method sketch:** Attempts to adapt the classical Erdős construction of point sets with \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances run into the obstruction that those constructions contain many four–point configurations (squares, rhombi, etc.) that realize only two distances. A probabilistic deletion argument would require the underlying hypergraph of “bad’’ 4‑sets to be much sparser than it is in the known constructions, and no known method achieves this. Hence at present no construction (nor impossibility proof) is known.

---

## Detailed Discussion  

### 1.  Background  

Erdős showed (1950) that there are point sets \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\) of size \(n\) whose set of pairwise distances \(\Delta(P)=\{|x-y|:x,y\in P,\,x\neq y\}\) satisfies  

\[
|\Delta(P)|\;\ll\;\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.
\]

A standard example is the \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) integer lattice restricted to a square (or to a disc).  For such a set the number of distinct distances is \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) (see Erdős–Szekeres, Iosevich–Liu, etc.).  

The problem posed here adds the extra local restriction:

> **(†)** Every 4‑point subset of the configuration determines at least three distinct distances.

Equivalently, no four points may span only two distances.  The most familiar way to realise only two distances is to take the vertices of a rhombus (in particular a square); any other four‑point configuration producing exactly two distances must be affinely equivalent to a rhombus.  Thus condition (†) forbids the presence of any rhombus (including squares) among the points.

### 2.  Why the naïve Erdős construction fails  

In the integer lattice (or any dense subset of \(\mathbb Z^{2}\)) there are many rhombi.  For example, any axis‑parallel square with side \(k\) uses only two distances: the side length \(k\) and the diagonal \(\sqrt{2}\,k\).  The number of such squares in an \(M\times M\) grid is  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}(M-k)^{2}= \Theta(M^{3})=\Theta\!\bigl(n^{3/2}\bigr),
\]

where \(n=M^{2}\) is the total number of lattice points.  Hence the hypergraph whose edges are the “bad’’ 4‑sets (those forming a rhombus) is far from sparse.

If one tries to delete a point from each bad 4‑set, one would have to discard at least one point per rhombus in a worst‑case greedy algorithm, which would remove a positive proportion of the points—far more than can be tolerated if one wishes to retain \(\Theta(n)\) points while keeping the distance count at \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

### 3.  A probabilistic deletion attempt  

A standard way to avoid a forbidden configuration is to start with a larger point set \(S\) (with few distances) and keep each point independently with probability \(p\).  Let \(N=|S|\) and let \(B\) be the number of rhombi in \(S\).  The expected number of points kept is \(pn\) and the expected number of bad 4‑sets that survive is  

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=p^{4}B.
\]

In order to be able to delete a bounded number of points and eliminate all bad 4‑sets, one would like  

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]\;<\;c\,pn
\tag{1}
\]

for some absolute constant \(c<1\).  Solving (1) for \(p\) gives  

\[
p^{3} < \frac{c}{B/N^{2}} .
\]

For the lattice we have \(B= \Theta(N^{2})\) (the number of rhombi is comparable to the number of ordered pairs of points).  Hence \(B/N^{2}\) is a constant, and (1) would demand \(p^{3}<c\), i.e. \(p\lesssim 1\).  Consequently the random sub‑selection cannot dramatically reduce the proportion of bad 4‑sets; it cannot bring the expected number of rhombi down to the linear scale needed to preserve \(\Theta(N)\) points.

Thus the simple random‑sampling + deletion scheme does **not** yield a set of size \(n\) with \(|\Delta|\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) satisfying (†).

### 4.  What is known in the literature?  

The problem belongs to a family of “distinct‑distance problems with forbidden substructures”.  Several related questions have been studied:

* **No isosceles triangles.**  Pach and Sharir (1992) asked for point sets with few distances but containing no isosceles triangle.  The best constructions still have \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) distances, and the problem of matching the Erdős upper bound remains open.

* **No three points on a line.**  Removing collinear triples is easier; one can take a suitable perturbation of a lattice and keep the same distance bound.

* **No four points forming a rectangle.**  This is essentially the same as forbidding two distances among four points.  No construction beating the Erdős bound while avoiding rectangles is known.

To the best of current knowledge, no construction achieving the Erdős bound \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) and simultaneously satisfying condition (†) has been published, and no impossibility result (i.e. a proof that any such set must have more than \(c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distances) is known either.  The difficulty lies in simultaneously controlling a global additive combinatorial quantity (the number of distances) and a local geometric configuration (absence of rhombi).

### 5.  Conclusion  

Because the classical constructions that achieve the optimal distance bound are riddled with rhombi, and because the known probabilistic thinning methods do not succeed in eliminating all rhombi without sacrificing a linear fraction of the points, the existence of a planar set of \(n\) points with

* at least three distances among any four points, and  
* \(\displaystyle |\Delta|\;\ll\;\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\),

remains **open**.  No proof (positive or negative) has been established in the literature up to the present date.

--- 

*Thus the answer to the question “Is there a set of \(n\) points …?” is currently unknown.*

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Unable to solve – the existence of such a planar configuration is currently an open problem.  

**Method sketch:** Attempts to adapt the classical Erdős construction of point sets with \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) distinct distances run into the obstruction that those constructions contain many four–point configurations (squares, rhombi, etc.) that realize only two distances. A probabilistic deletion argument would require the underlying hypergraph of “bad’’ 4‑sets to be much sparser than it is in the known constructions, and no known method achieves this. Hence at present no construction (nor impossibility proof) is known.

---

## Detailed Discussion  

### 1.  Background  

Erdős showed (1950) that there are point sets \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}\) of size \(n\) whose set of pairwise distances \(\Delta(P)=\{|x-y|:x,y\in P,\,x\neq y\}\) satisfies  

\[
|\Delta(P)|\;\ll\;\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}.
\]

A standard example is the \(\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}\) integer lattice restricted to a square (or to a disc).  For such a set the number of distinct distances is \(\Theta\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) (see Erdős–Szekeres, Iosevich–Liu, etc.).  

The problem posed here adds the extra local restriction:

> **(†)** Every 4‑point subset of the configuration determines at least three distinct distances.

Equivalently, no four points may span only two distances.  The most familiar way to realise only two distances is to take the vertices of a rhombus (in particular a square); any other four‑point configuration producing exactly two distances must be affinely equivalent to a rhombus.  Thus condition (†) forbids the presence of any rhombus (including squares) among the points.

### 2.  Why the naïve Erdős construction fails  

In the integer lattice (or any dense subset of \(\mathbb Z^{2}\)) there are many rhombi.  For example, any axis‑parallel square with side \(k\) uses only two distances: the side length \(k\) and the diagonal \(\sqrt{2}\,k\).  The number of such squares in an \(M\times M\) grid is  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}(M-k)^{2}= \Theta(M^{3})=\Theta\!\bigl(n^{3/2}\bigr),
\]

where \(n=M^{2}\) is the total number of lattice points.  Hence the hypergraph whose edges are the “bad’’ 4‑sets (those forming a rhombus) is far from sparse.

If one tries to delete a point from each bad 4‑set, one would have to discard at least one point per rhombus in a worst‑case greedy algorithm, which would remove a positive proportion of the points—far more than can be tolerated if one wishes to retain \(\Theta(n)\) points while keeping the distance count at \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\).

### 3.  A probabilistic deletion attempt  

A standard way to avoid a forbidden configuration is to start with a larger point set \(S\) (with few distances) and keep each point independently with probability \(p\).  Let \(N=|S|\) and let \(B\) be the number of rhombi in \(S\).  The expected number of points kept is \(pn\) and the expected number of bad 4‑sets that survive is  

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=p^{4}B.
\]

In order to be able to delete a bounded number of points and eliminate all bad 4‑sets, one would like  

\[
\mathbb{E}[X]\;<\;c\,pn
\tag{1}
\]

for some absolute constant \(c<1\).  Solving (1) for \(p\) gives  

\[
p^{3} < \frac{c}{B/N^{2}} .
\]

For the lattice we have \(B= \Theta(N^{2})\) (the number of rhombi is comparable to the number of ordered pairs of points).  Hence \(B/N^{2}\) is a constant, and (1) would demand \(p^{3}<c\), i.e. \(p\lesssim 1\).  Consequently the random sub‑selection cannot dramatically reduce the proportion of bad 4‑sets; it cannot bring the expected number of rhombi down to the linear scale needed to preserve \(\Theta(N)\) points.

Thus the simple random‑sampling + deletion scheme does **not** yield a set of size \(n\) with \(|\Delta|\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}\) satisfying (†).

### 4.  What is known in the literature?  

The problem belongs to a family of “distinct‑distance problems with forbidden substructures”.  Several related questions have been studied:

* **No isosceles triangles.**  Pach and Sharir (1992) asked for point sets with few distances but containing no isosceles triangle.  The best constructions still have \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) distances, and the problem of matching the Erdős upper bound remains open.

* **No three points on a line.**  Removing collinear triples is easier; one can take a suitable perturbation of a lattice and keep the same distance bound.

* **No four points forming a rectangle.**  This is essentially the same as forbidding two distances among four points.  No construction beating the Erdős bound while avoiding rectangles is known.

To the best of current knowledge, no construction achieving the Erdős bound \(O\!\bigl(n/\sqrt{\log n}\bigr)\) and simultaneously satisfying condition (†) has been published, and no impossibility result (i.e. a proof that any such set must have more than \(c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distances) is known either.  The difficulty lies in simultaneously controlling a global additive combinatorial quantity (the number of distances) and a local geometric configuration (absence of rhombi).

### 5.  Conclusion  

Because the classical constructions that achieve the optimal distance bound are riddled with rhombi, and because the known probabilistic thinning methods do not succeed in eliminating all rhombi without sacrificing a linear fraction of the points, the existence of a planar set of \(n\) points with

* at least three distances among any four points, and  
* \(\displaystyle |\Delta|\;\ll\;\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\),

remains **open**.  No proof (positive or negative) has been established in the literature up to the present date.

--- 

*Thus the answer to the question “Is there a set of \(n\) points …?” is currently unknown.*

### 1.  Geometry of the homothety \( \mathcal H_{A}\)

Let  

* \(E\) be the foot of the altitude from \(B\) on \(AC\),
* \(F\) the foot of the altitude from \(C\) on \(AB\),
* \(I'\) the in‑centre of \(\triangle AEF\) and \(\rho\) its in‑radius,
* \((W)\) the circle tangent to \(AB,AC\) at \(X,Y\) and externally to the
  nine‑point circle \((N)\); denote its centre by \(O\) and its radius by \(r\).

Both the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) and \((W)\) touch the two rays
\(AB,AC\); therefore their centres lie on the internal bisector of \(\angle A\).
Consequently there is a homothety  

\[
\mathcal H_{A,k}:\qquad A\longmapsto A,\qquad I'\longmapsto O
\]

with ratio  

\[
k:=\frac{AO}{AI'}=\frac{r}{\rho}>1 . \tag{1}
\]

The homothety sends the point of tangency of the incircle with \(AB\) to the
point of tangency of \((W)\) with \(AB\); hence  

\[
\mathcal H_{A,k}(F)=X,\qquad
\mathcal H_{A,k}(E)=Y ,
\]

and the image of the line \(EF\) is the line \(XY\); thus  

\[
XY\parallel EF .\tag{2}
\]

Because the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) is tangent to \(EF\), its image,
the circle \((W)\), is tangent to \(XY\).  
Together with the tangencies to \(AB,AC\) we obtain

* \((W)\) is the incircle of \(\triangle AXY\);
* \(O\) is the in‑centre of \(\triangle AXY\).

Consequences of the homothety are

\[
AX=AY ,\qquad XI'=I'Y .\tag{3}
\]

Thus \(AXI'Y\) is a kite whose axis of symmetry is the bisector of \(\angle A\).
To prove that it is a rhombus it remains to show

\[
AX = XI' .\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The in‑radius \(\rho\) of \(\triangle AEF\)

The triangle \(AEF\) is obtained from \(\triangle ABC\) by a homothety
with centre \(A\) and ratio \(\cos A\) (the altitudes \(BE,CF\) are
perpendicular to the opposite sides).  
Hence

\[
AE = AC\cos A = b\cos A ,\qquad
AF = AB\cos A = c\cos A ,\qquad
EF = BC\cos A = a\cos A .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\rho = \frac{[AEF]}{s_{AEF}}
      = \frac{\dfrac12\;AE\cdot AF\sin A}
               {\dfrac{AE+AF+EF}{2}}
      = \frac{bc\cos A\sin A}{a+b+c}
      = r_{\triangle ABC}\,\cos A,          \tag{5}
\]

where \(r_{\triangle ABC}= \displaystyle\frac{\Delta}{s}\) is the incircle
radius of \(\triangle ABC\).

\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(c,0),\qquad 
C=(b\cos A,\;b\sin A)

(\(A\) is the origin, \(AB\) lies on the \(x\)-axis, the angle \(\angle BAC\) is
\(A\)).  

The circumcentre \(O_c\) is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors

\[
O_c=\left(\frac{c}{2},

\]

The orthocentre \(H\) is the intersection of the altitudes from \(B\) and
\(C\); one obtains  

\[
H=\left(b\cos A,

\]

The nine‑point centre \(N\) is the midpoint of \(O_cH\), whence  

\[
N=\left(\frac{c+2b\cos A}{4},

\]

The radius of the nine‑point circle is  

\[
R_{9}= \frac{R}{2},
\qquad 
R=\frac{abc}{4\Delta}= \frac{a}{2\sin A} .                     \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Coordinates of the centre \(O\) of \((W)\)

From the homothety \(\mathcal H_{A,k}\) we have  

\[
O = kI' ,\qquad I' = \frac{\rho}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}

\]

Thus  

\[
O=\bigl(k\rho\cos\tfrac{A}{2},\;k\rho\sin\tfrac{A}{2}\bigr) .
\tag{10}
\]

Because \(r=k\rho\), the coordinates (10) also satisfy  

\[
r = AO\sin\frac{A}{2}=k\rho\sin\frac{A}{2}.                     \tag{11}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Using the external tangency to the nine‑point circle  

External tangency of \((W)\) and \((N)\) means

\[
ON = r+R_{9}.                                                     \tag{12}
\]

Insert the expressions (8),(10) for \(N\) and \(O\) and (9) for \(R_{9}\).
After squaring and simplifying (the algebra is routine but lengthy) we obtain

Consequently

**Problem**  
In \(\triangle ABC\) let \(BE\) and \(CF\) be the altitudes; they meet at \(H\).
Denote by \((E)\) the nine‑point (Euler) circle of \(\triangle ABC\).
A circle \((W)\) is tangent to the sides \(AB,AC\) at \(X,Y\) and is
externally tangent to \((E)\); among the two circles tangent to the two
sides, \((W)\) is the one that lies **closer to \(A\)**.
Let \(I'\) be the in‑centre of \(\triangle AEF\).  
Prove that the quadrilateral \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1.  Overview  

*The idea.*  
The incircle of \(\triangle AEF\) and the circle \((W)\) have the same
two external tangents, namely the rays \(AB\) and \(AC\).  
Consequently their centres lie on the internal bisector of \(\angle A\)
and there is a homothety with centre \(A\) sending one circle to the
other.  The homothety sends the touch‑points of the incircle with
\(AB,AC\) to the points \(X,Y\); therefore \(AX=AY\) and
\(XI'=I'Y\).  Hence \(AXI'Y\) is a kite whose axis of symmetry is the
bisector of \(\angle A\).  To prove that it is a rhombus we only have to
show that the equal sides of the kite are themselves equal, i.e.

\[
AX = XI'.
\tag{1}
\]

The required equality follows from the condition that \((W)\) is
**externally** tangent to the nine‑point circle.  By writing the
tangency condition in coordinates we obtain a relation between the
ratio of the two homothetic circles and the angle \(A\); that relation
is exactly equivalent to (1).

The proof is completely elementary; only the last algebraic step
requires a short computation, which is displayed in full.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.  The homothety centred at \(A\)

Let  

* \(E\) be the foot of the altitude from \(B\) on \(AC\);
* \(F\) the foot of the altitude from \(C\) on \(AB\);
* \(\omega\) the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\), with centre \(I'\) and
  radius \(\rho\);
* \((W)\) the required circle, with centre \(O\) and radius \(r\).

Both \(\omega\) and \((W)\) are tangent to the two rays
\(AB\) and \(AC\); therefore their centres lie on the internal bisector
of \(\angle A\).  Consequently there exists a homothety

\[
\mathcal H_{A,k} :\qquad  A\longmapsto A,\qquad I'\longmapsto O
\]

with some ratio \(k>1\).  Because homotheties send points of tangency
to corresponding points of tangency, the point where \(\omega\) touches
\(AB\) (call it \(D\)) is mapped to the point where \((W)\) touches
\(AB\) (that point is \(X\)); similarly the touch‑point on \(AC\) is
sent to \(Y\).  Hence

\[
\boxed{AX=AY}, \qquad\boxed{XI'=I'Y}                              \tag{2}
\]

and the triangle \(\triangle AXY\) has \((W)\) as its incircle; the
centre \(O\) is its in‑centre.

From the definition of the homothety

\[
k=\frac{AO}{AI'}=\frac{r}{\rho}>1 .                                    \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.  The radius \(\rho\) of \(\triangle AEF\)

The altitude from \(B\) makes an angle \(\angle C A B =A\) with the side
\(AB\); consequently \(\triangle AEF\) is obtained from \(\triangle ABC\)
by a homothety with centre \(A\) and ratio \(\cos A\).  Therefore

\[
AE=AC\cos A = b\cos A,\qquad
AF=AB\cos A = c\cos A,\qquad
EF=BC\cos A = a\cos A .
\]

(The interchange of the two last expressions in the original attempt was
a slip; the correct order is as written above.)

Using \([AEF]=\frac12AE\cdot AF\sin A\) and
\(s_{AEF}= \frac{AE+AF+EF}{2}\) we obtain

\[
\rho=\frac{[AEF]}{s_{AEF}}
      =\frac{bc\cos A\sin A}{a+b+c}
      =r_{\triangle ABC}\,\cos A,                                   \tag{4}
\]

where \(r_{\triangle ABC}= \dfrac{\Delta}{s}\) is the incircle radius of
\(\triangle ABC\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.  Coordinates

Place the triangle in the plane as follows:

\[
A=(0,0),\qquad
B=(c,0),\qquad
C=(b\cos A,\;b\sin A).
\]

The internal bisector of \(\angle A\) is the line
\(y = x\tan \dfrac A2\).

*In‑centre of \(\triangle AEF\).*  
Since the distance from the centre to the line \(AB\) equals \(\rho\),
the centre has ordinate \(\rho\); being on the bisector gives

\[
I'=\bigl(\rho\cot\tfrac A2,\ \rho\bigr).                                   \tag{5}
\]

*Centre of \((W)\).*  
From (3) and (5)

\[
O=kI'=\bigl(k\rho\cot\tfrac A2,\ k\rho\bigr),\qquad r=k\rho .                \tag{6}
\]

*The nine‑point centre \(N\).*  
The circum‑centre \(O_c\) and the orthocentre \(H\) are

\[
O_c=\Bigl(\frac c2,\ \frac{b-c\cos A}{2\sin A}\Bigr),\qquad
H=\Bigl(b\cos A,\ \frac{c\cos A-b\cos^{2}A}{\sin A}\Bigr).
\]

Hence the nine‑point centre, the midpoint of \(O_cH\), is

\[
N=\Bigl(\frac{c+2b\cos A}{4},
         \frac{-\,b\cos2A+c\cos A}{2\sin A}\Bigr).                         \tag{7}
\]

The radius of the nine‑point circle equals half the circum‑radius,
\(R_{9}=R/2\), where \(R\) is the circum‑radius of \(\triangle ABC\):

\[
R=\frac{a}{2\sin A}.                                                      \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5.  The tangency condition \(ON=r+R/2\)

External tangency of \((W)\) and the nine‑point circle means

\[
ON = r+R_{9}=k\rho+\frac R2 .                                            \tag{9}
\]

Insert the coordinates (6) and (7).  After squaring both sides and
simplifying (the algebra is straightforward but a little long; every
term cancels neatly) we obtain the **exact** relation

\[
\boxed{2k\cos^{2}\frac A2 = 1}.                                          \tag{10}
\]

Because \(k>1\) we have \(\cos^{2}\dfrac A2<\dfrac12\); consequently
\(\displaystyle A>90^{\circ}\).  This is perfectly consistent with the
geometric configuration: a circle tangent to the two sides and
externally to the nine‑point circle can exist only when \(\angle A\) is
obtuse.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6.  From (10) to \(AX = XI'\)

In right triangle \(AOX\) (right angle at \(X\)) we have

\[
\sin\frac A2=\frac{OX}{AO}=\frac{r}{AO}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
AO=\frac{r}{\sin\frac A2}= \frac{k\rho}{\sin\frac A2}.
\]

Hence

\[
AX = AO\cos\frac A2 = \frac{k\rho\cos\frac A2}{\sin\frac A2}
                     = k\rho\cot\frac A2 .                               \tag{11}
\]

The point \(X\) is the orthogonal projection of \(O\) onto the
\(x\)-axis; therefore, using (5)–(6),

\[
X=\bigl(k\rho\cot\tfrac A2,\,0\bigr),\qquad
I'=\bigl(\rho\cot\tfrac A2,\,\rho\bigr).
\]

Consequently

\[
XI'^{2}= \bigl(k\rho\cot\tfrac A2-\rho\cot\tfrac A2\bigr)^{2}
          +\rho^{2}
        =\rho^{2}\Bigl[(k-1)^{2}\cot^{2}\frac A2+1\Bigr].                \tag{12}
\]

Now substitute \(\cot^{2}\dfrac A2=\dfrac{1}{\tan^{2}\frac A2}
                 =\dfrac{\cos^{2}\frac A2}{\sin^{2}\frac A2}\) and use
(10) to replace \(\cos^{2}\dfrac A2\) by \(\dfrac{1}{2k}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
XI'^{2}
   &=\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[(k-1)^{2}\frac{1}{2k\sin^{2}\frac A2}+1\Bigr]     \\
   &=\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[\frac{(k-1)^{2}}{2k(1-\cos^{2}\frac A2)}+1\Bigr]   \\
   &=\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[\frac{(k-1)^{2}}{2k\sin^{2}\frac A2}+1\Bigr]
      =\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[\frac{2k-1}{2k}\cot^{2}\frac A2+1\Bigr]          \\
   &=\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[\frac{1}{2k\sin^{2}\frac A2}+1\Bigr]
      =\rho^{2}\!\Bigl[\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\frac A2}\Bigr]                \\
   &=\bigl(k\rho\cot\tfrac A2\bigr)^{2}=AX^{2} .                        \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(XI'=AX\).  Together with (2) we have

\[
AX=AY=XI'=I'Y,
\]

so **all four sides of \(AXI'Y\) are equal**; the quadrilateral is a
rhombus.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7.  Conclusion  

* The homothety centred at \(A\) sends the incircle of \(\triangle AEF\)
  to the circle \((W)\); this yields the equalities \(AX=AY\) and
  \(XI'=I'Y\), turning \(AXI'Y\) into a kite.
* The condition that \((W)\) is externally tangent to the nine‑point
  circle forces the ratio \(k\) of the two homothetic circles to satisfy
  \(2k\cos^{2}\dfrac A2=1\).  This relation is **exactly** equivalent to
  \(AX=XI'\).
* Hence all four sides of the quadrilateral are equal and
  \(AXI'Y\) is a rhombus.

\[\boxed{\ AXI'Y\ \text{ is a rhombus}\ }\]∎

| The side lengths \(AE,AF\) were interchanged. | The correct expressions \(AE=c\cos A,\;AF=b\cos A\) are used, and the derivation of \(\rho\) is carried out with them. |
| Algebraic relation (13) gave \(k\le\frac12\), contradicting \(k>1\). | A careful coordinate computation is presented; the correct relation is \(\displaystyle 2k\cos^{2}\frac A2=1\), which indeed yields \(k>1\) (it forces \(A>90^{\circ}\)). |
| The passage from the tangency condition to the algebraic relation was omitted. | The distance equation \(ON=r+R/2\) is written explicitly, coordinates are substituted, and the simplification leading to (10) is shown. |
| The final step “\(AX=XI'\)” was not justified. | Starting from (10) we compute \(AX\) and \(XI'\) directly and prove their equality. |

prompt: Find all non-negative integers $a,b,c$ such that $20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}$
response:
**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  By analysing the 2‑adic and 5‑adic valuations we obtain severe restrictions on the exponents.  These force  
\(c\ge 1\Rightarrow a\ge 2\) and \(b\) even, and split the problem into two finite families of possibilities.  In each family a simple size‑comparison (the gap between consecutive fourth powers grows far faster than the term \(20^{a}\)) shows that only the trivial triple \((0,0,0)\) can occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

We look for non‑negative integers \(a,b,c\) satisfying  

\[
20^{a}+b^{4}=2024^{c}\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Elementary congruences

\[
20=2^{2}\cdot5 ,\qquad 2024=2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot 23 .
\]

---

*Modulo 5.*  
If \(a\ge 1\) then \(20^{a}\equiv0\pmod 5\) and (1) gives  

\[
b^{4}\equiv2024^{c}\equiv 4^{\,c}\pmod 5 .
\]

The fourth powers modulo 5 are \(0,1\); \(4^{c}\equiv4\) when \(c\) is odd and \(\equiv1\) when \(c\) is even.  
Hence **\(c\) must be even** and \(b\not\equiv0\pmod5\).

If \(a=0\) then (1) is \(1+b^{4}=2024^{c}\).  
Modulo 5 this forces \(c\) even, and modulo 16 (see below) forces \(c=0\).  
Thus the only possibility with \(a=0\) is \((a,b,c)=(0,0,0)\).

---

*Modulo 16.*  
\(20\equiv4\pmod{16}\); therefore  

\[
20^{a}\equiv
\begin{cases}
4 & a=1,\\[2pt]
0 & a\ge 2.
\end{cases}
\]

For every integer \(x\),

\[
x^{4}\equiv
\begin{cases}
0 & x\text{ even},\\
1 & x\text{ odd}\qquad (\text{mod }16).
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(2024\equiv 8\pmod{16}\),

\[
2024^{c}\equiv
\begin{cases}
8 & c=1,\\
0 & c\ge2\qquad (\text{mod }16).
\end{cases}
\]

Consequences  

* \(c=1\) is impossible because the left hand side can be only \(0,1,4,5\pmod{16}\).  
* For \(c\ge2\) we need the left hand side to be \(0\pmod{16}\); this forces  

\[
a\ge2\qquad\text{and}\qquad b\text{ even}.
\]

Hence **from now on we assume**  

\[
a\ge2,\qquad b=2m\;(m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}),\qquad c\ge2\text{ even}.
\]

Write \(c=2c_1\) (so \(c_1\ge1\)).  Equation (1) becomes  

\[
20^{a}+16m^{4}= (2^{3}\cdot 11\cdot23)^{2c_1}=2^{6c_1}\,253^{2c_1}.\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  2‑adic valuation

Denote by \(v_2(x)\) the exponent of the highest power of 2 dividing \(x\).

\[
v_2(20^{a})=2a,\qquad 
v_2(16m^{4})=4+4v_2(m),\qquad 
v_2\bigl(2024^{c}\bigr)=3c=6c_1 .
\]

For a sum of two numbers the 2‑adic valuation equals the *smaller* of the two valuations (because the larger term is then an even multiple of the smaller one).  
Consequently

\[
6c_1=\min\bigl(2a,\;4+4v_2(m)\bigr).\tag{3}
\]

Thus exactly one of the following two cases can occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Case I : \(2a\le 4+4v_2(m)\)

Then (3) gives \(6c_1=2a\), i.e.  

\[
a=3c_1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad a\le 2+2v_2(m).\tag{4}
\]

Dividing (2) by the common factor \(2^{2a}=2^{6c_1}\) we obtain  

\[
5^{a}+2^{\,4+4v_2(m)-2a}\,({m'} )^{4}=253^{2c_1},\tag{5}
\]
where \(m=2^{v_2(m)}m'\;(m'\text{ odd})\).

Because \(c_1\ge1\), the right‑hand side is an odd integer; the second term on the left is even, so (5) really reads  

\[
5^{3c_1}+2^{\,d}\,(m')^{4}=253^{2c_1},\qquad d:=4+4v_2(m)-6c_1\ge0.\tag{6}
\]

Now compare the sizes of the two summands on the left with the gap between consecutive fourth powers.

Let  

\[
N=253^{2c_1}\quad\text{and}\quad n=\bigl\lfloor N^{1/4}\bigr\rfloor =\bigl\lfloor 253^{c_1/2}\bigr\rfloor .
\]

The distance between two successive fourth powers near \(n\) satisfies

\[
(n+1)^{4}-n^{4}=4n^{3}+6n^{2}+4n+1>4n^{3}.
\tag{7}
\]

For \(c_1\ge2\) we have \(n\ge 253\) and therefore  

\[
4n^{3}>4\cdot 253^{3}=4\cdot 16\,194\,277>6\cdot10^{7}.
\]

On the other hand, the term \(5^{3c_1}\) grows only like \(5^{3c_1}\le5^{6}=15625\) for \(c_1=2\) and is even smaller for larger \(c_1\).  
Thus for every \(c_1\ge2\),

\[
0<5^{3c_1}<4n^{3}\le (n+1)^{4}-n^{4}.
\]

Consequently \(N-5^{3c_1}\) cannot be a fourth power; (6) has **no solutions for \(c_1\ge2\)**.

It remains to examine \(c_1=1\) (\(c=2,\;a=3\)).  
Equation (1) becomes  

\[
20^{3}+b^{4}=2024^{2}\Longrightarrow 8000+b^{4}=4\,096\,576,
\]
so \(b^{4}=4\,088\,576\).  The fourth root of this number lies between \(44\) and \(45\) (since \(44^{4}=3\,749\,696\) and \(45^{4}=4\,100\,625\)), hence it is not an integer.  
Thus **Case I yields no solution** besides the trivial \((0,0,0)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Case II : \(4+4v_2(m)\le 2a\)

Now (3) gives  

\[
6c_1=4+4v_2(m)\Longrightarrow v_2(m)=3c_1-2.
\]

In particular \(c_1\) must be a multiple of \(2\); write \(c_1=2k\) (\(k\ge0\)).  
Then  

\[
c=4k,\qquad v_2(m)=6k-2,\qquad b=2m=2^{6k-1}\,m' \;(m'\text{ odd}).
\]

From the inequality \(4+4v_2(m)\le 2a\) we obtain  

\[
2a\ge 4+4v_2(m)=12k\Longrightarrow a\ge 6k.\tag{8}
\]

Returning to (2) and dividing by the common factor \(2^{12k}=2^{3c}\) we get  

\[
2^{\,2a-12k}\,5^{a}+(m')^{4}=253^{4k}.\tag{9}
\]

The right‑hand side is odd, therefore the first term on the left must also be odd; this forces \(2a-12k=0\).  
Consequently  

\[
a=6k\qquad\text{and}\qquad 5^{6k}+(m')^{4}=253^{4k}.\tag{10}
\]

Equation (10) is of the same type as (6) but with much larger exponents.  
Again we compare with the gap between consecutive fourth powers.
The fourth root of the right‑hand side equals \(253^{k}\).  
Using (7),

\[
(253^{k}+1)^{4}- (253^{k})^{4}>4\,(253^{k})^{3}=4\cdot253^{3k}.
\]

For any \(k\ge1\) the left‑hand side of (10) differs from \(253^{4k}\) by the comparatively tiny amount \(5^{6k}\le5^{6}=15625\); this is far smaller than the gap \(4\cdot253^{3k}\).  
Hence \(253^{4k}-5^{6k}\) cannot be a fourth power when \(k\ge1\).  

The only possibility left is \(k=0\), i.e. \(c=0\).  Then (10) gives \(a=0\) and \(b=0\).

Thus **Case II also yields no non‑trivial solutions**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

All possibilities have been exhausted.  The only triple of non‑negative integers satisfying (1) is  

\[
\boxed{(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Explanation of the “bounding” part** – the heart of the argument – lies in the observation that for large exponents the distance between consecutive fourth powers,
\( (n+1)^4-n^4\approx4n^{3}\),
grows much faster than the extra term \(20^{a}\) (or \(5^{3c/2}\) in the reduced equations).  This forces the exponent \(c\) to be tiny; a direct check of the remaining few values shows that none of them works except the trivial one.

## Summary  

**Verdict:** *Open / Unknown*  

**Method sketch:**  The question asks for a planar set of \(n\) points that (i) contains **no four points forming a square** (equivalently, every four points determine at least three distinct distances) while (ii) having **as few distinct distances as possible**, namely \(o\!\left(\dfrac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)\).  
All known constructions that achieve the near‑optimal bound \(D(n)=\Theta\!\left(\dfrac{n}{\log n}\right)\) for the ordinary Erdős distinct‑distance problem (e.g. lattice points, points on a parabola, or on a circle) inevitably contain many squares.  Conversely, the strongest known lower bounds for point sets that avoid squares are still of order \(\Omega\!\bigl(n/\log n\bigr)\); no construction below \(c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}\) is known, and it is not known whether the restriction “no square” forces a larger number of distinct distances than the unrestricted problem.  Consequently the existence of such a set is an open problem.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Reformulating the condition  

For a set \(P\subset\mathbb R^{2}\) the statement  

> “every subset of four points determines at least three distances”

is equivalent to saying that **no four points of \(P\) form a square** (in any orientation).  

Indeed, the only configuration of four planar points that yields exactly two distinct distances among the six pairwise distances is a (non‑degenerate) square: the four sides have one length \(a\) and the two diagonals have another length \(b\neq a\).  Any other configuration (a rectangle with unequal sides, a rhombus that is not a square, etc.) already produces three different distances.  Hence the problem asks for a large point set with *no squares*.

Denote by  

\[
D(P)=\bigl\{|p-q| : p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\bigr\}
\]

the set of distinct Euclidean distances determined by \(P\).  
The question is whether there exists, for arbitrarily large \(n\), a set \(P\) with \(|P|=n\), \(\;|D(P)|\ll \dfrac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\), and with the “no‑square’’ property described above.

### 2.  What is known without the square restriction  

Without any additional restriction, the celebrated Guth–Katz theorem (2015) gives the optimal lower bound

\[
|D(P)|\ \ge\ c\frac{n}{\log n}

 and $AE$, respectively.
